text: Q# looks unfamiliar for about ten minutes and then starts feeling like a strict, quantum-aware cousin of C#. Before you write anything that touches a qubit, you need the classical skeleton underneath it — none of what follows is quantum yet, but all of it is load-bearing for every lesson after this one.

Five things to get solid: namespaces, which organize Q# code the way a Python module groups functions; the real split between operation and function; let versus mutable bindings and Q#'s core type annotations; arrays and Range; and control flow, including one loop shape with no common classical equivalent.

Every Q# file lives inside a namespace block, grouping related operations and functions. Namespaces don't have to match folder or file names exactly, but by convention a project's entry namespace matches the project name, and you open a namespace to use its contents elsewhere — similar to a Python import.

Q# draws a hard line Python never needs to. A function is purely classical and deterministic — same inputs, same outputs, no qubits touched. An operation is anything that can have quantum effects or non-deterministic behavior — allocating or measuring qubits, or calling another operation. The compiler enforces this: you cannot call an operation from inside a function, because a function's whole contract is deterministic, side-effect-free, and operations break that contract by definition.

let creates an immutable binding — once set, it can't be reassigned. mutable creates a binding you can later update with set. The core primitive types are Int, Double, Bool, String, Qubit, and Result, the outcome of a measurement. And Unit is Q#'s "nothing to return" type, used whenever an operation's whole point is a side effect rather than a value — the equivalent of void in C# or None in Python.

repeat-until is the one loop shape with no common classical equivalent in mainstream languages — closest to a do-while, but built specifically for retrying a quantum measurement until you get the outcome you need. The body always runs at least once, then the until condition is checked; if it's false, it loops again. Notice outcome had to be declared mutable before the repeat block, because set inside the loop body needs a variable that already exists in an outer scope.
Next lesson, you put every piece of this syntax to work in one real program: allocate a qubit, apply a gate, measure it, and check the exact math behind what it should produce.
